AI Summary

Three papers this fortnight land directly on lab systems. Wan et al. profile paired epigenomes and transcriptomes from multiple myeloma patients and find that genome-wide methylation loss opens LINE-1 promoters that generate chimeric transcripts with adjacent oncogenes — the TE-as-alternative-promoter mechanism of LTR10 in colorectal cancer, in a different tumor type, with KRAB-containing zinc finger proteins abnormally low in exactly the samples where L1 activity is high. Their high-L1 tumors suppress interferon and genome-defense pathways rather than activating them, which is the opposite of the viral-mimicry expectation and the most interesting loose end in this digest. Garza et al. supply the correlative human-tissue case for the other direction: over a thousand TEs, including LINE-1s and ERVs, expressed in cell-type- and region-specific patterns across postmortem brain, with increased TE expression in substantia nigra and putamen microglia and neurons — but not amygdala or prefrontal cortex — tracking a regional innate immune response, and the TE–interferon link confirmed in pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia and neurons. Bravo et al. close the causal gap with a gain-of-function test: transient L1Hs overexpression in primary human IMR-90 fibroblasts remodels transcriptome, proteome and secretome and engages cell-cycle and interferon pathways, while the authors argue the response is neither plain senescence nor reducible to antiviral signaling, and that independent L1 elements give both shared and distinct responses.

The silencing side is unusually well covered this cycle. Deng et al. show how a host reads a nascent LTR retrotransposon transcript as a silencing signal: Puf68 binds poly-U tracts in the pre-tRNA 3' trailer, the complex base-pairs with the element's primer binding site, and Puf68 recruits Su(var)3-9 to deposit H3K9me3 — sufficient to nucleate heterochromatin de novo at ectopically integrated LTR elements. Gronbaek et al. find the Drosophila germline reconfigures its piRNA pathway mid-development, from promoter-driven clusters silencing the subset of TE families competent in mitotic germ cells to heterochromatic dual-strand clusters (via Moonshiner, Kipferl, Nxf3 and Bootlegger) as more families become active in nurse cells. Porquet et al. name AP-1 as the axis linking inflammatory stress to TE activation in hematopoietic stem cells: transient OSKM reprogramming closes AP-1-enriched chromatin and represses TEs, AP-1 inhibition prevents LPS-induced TE activation, and reverse transcriptase inhibition improves aged HSC function. That is the same transcription factor family that drives LTR10 enhancers downstream of MAPK in the lab's colorectal system, here in a stem cell compartment with an aging rather than oncogenic readout. Coll-Tane et al. round the theme out with an H3K9 methyltransferase phenotype in which no TE involvement is invoked at all — EHMT1/G9a maintaining sleep through developmental ROS and methionine homeostasis in insulin-producing cells.

The strongest convergence in this digest puts endogenous double-stranded RNA and m6A on a single axis. Johnson et al. show chronic type II interferon drives tumor growth by releasing double-stranded mitochondrial RNA that triggers a type I response, the two synergizing through immunosuppressive prostaglandin synthesis — signal duration deciding whether interferon attacks or shields a tumor. Arco-Hierves et al. place METTL3-dependent surveillance of mitochondrial RNA upstream of the epithelial interferon signature in lupus and Sjögren's disease, and Hu et al. show extruded mtRNA itself carries m6A, with the m6A machinery governing its cytoplasmic retention time and its engagement of RIG-I. Vlachogiannis et al. then make the pharmacology concrete: the METTL3 inhibitor STM2457 reverses TGF-β-driven profibrotic transcription in systemic sclerosis fibroblasts, in patients whose PBMCs show the writer complex upregulated, global m6A doubled, and marks redistributed from 3' UTRs into coding sequence. Substitute TE-derived transcripts for mitochondrial ones and this is the lab's epitranscriptomics question exactly — m6A as the tag deciding whether an endogenous structured RNA is tolerated or sensed. On the sensor side, Wang et al. identify the metabolite FAD occupying the catalytic pockets of both cGAS and RIG-I as an endogenous brake on self-nucleic-acid sensing, and Garikapati et al. split the CBP/p300 pair — cytoplasmic p300 interrupting TBK1–IRF3 while CBP is the chromatin-recruited coactivator tracking H3K27ac gain — which changes which perturbation to reach for when testing whether an interferon-inducible TE-derived enhancer is coactivator-dependent.

On regulatory architecture, Majumder et al. dissect the super enhancer between HLA-DR and HLA-DQ into five microelements and show they compete: deleting HLA-DRB1 proximal promoter elements raises HLA-DQ expression by co-opting region D, so absolute MHC-II levels are set by microelements contending for one enhancer. That is enhancer-microelement resolution at a polymorphic immune locus — the scale at which a TE insertion would act. Boulanger et al. show cis-regulatory elements share single-molecule accessibility across chromatin loops rather than firing independently, and Ye et al. identify hnRNPK condensates as the RNA-binding link between enhancer and promoter transcripts — a reason enhancer transcription from an ERV or LTR copy might be functional rather than incidental. For structural variation as regulatory variation, Waseem et al. reconstruct human-specific expansion and remodeling of the K111 endogenous retrovirus at acrocentric nucleolar organizer regions from complete primate genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies and trios, catching de novo sequence exchange within a single generation, while Merenciano et al. show two polymorphic intronic TE insertions amplify oxidative-stress induction of Mrp4 and inaE in cis in Drosophila suzukii — effects an earlier global analysis had missed. Method-side, Michielsen et al. bring spatial isoform sequencing to 500-nm single-cell resolution and show many spatial isoform signals are not explained by cell-type composition, and Rosen et al. deliver IGVF-standard MPRA formats and pipelines — the assay that turns a candidate TE-derived enhancer into a measurement, now comparable across studies.
